a: When you sit at a ruler's table to eat
t: Amenemope's chapter on the governor's table
p: 23:1–3 has a close cousin in the twenty-third chapter of the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.
b: The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope (see the notes at 22:17–21 for the whole parallel) has a chapter on eating with a high official. In Budge's translation it says: "Eat not thou bread in the presence of the Governor" and "Keep thy gaze fixed upon the vessel (platter?) which is before thee" (lines 460, 464). Proverbs shares the setting, the warning about appetite and the order to watch what is in front of you. It does not copy word for word: Amenemope warns that the governor may be as greedy as the sacred crocodiles, while Proverbs warns that the ruler's food itself "tells lies" (23:3). Most scholars think the Hebrew sage knew Amenemope, directly or through an Aramaic or Hebrew version, and reworked it for Israel's court. The parallels run from 22:17 to 23:11 and then stop.

a: pay close attention to what is in front of you
t: What, or who, is in front of you
p: The Hebrew can mean what is on the table or who is sitting across from you.
b: The Hebrew bin tavin 'et 'asher lefanekha doubles the verb "understand" for emphasis: "understand well what (or who) is before you." The relative word 'asher can point to a thing or a person. Read as "what", the advice is about the rich food (so Amenemope, "the vessel which is before thee"). Read as "who", it is about the ruler: know whom you are dealing with. Rashi and several modern commentators take it of the person. The Plain keeps the open "what is in front of you", which leaves room for both.
orig: בִּין תָּבִין אֶת־אֲשֶׁר לְפָנֶיךָ (bin tavin 'et 'asher lefanekha)

a: if you are a man of large appetite
p: Not a call to self-harm: a vivid order to restrain your appetite at a powerful man's table.
b: "Put a knife to your throat" is an image, not an instruction. The throat (lo'a, the gullet) is where appetite lives, and the man of "large appetite" is literally "an owner of a nefesh": nefesh here is the hungry throat or craving, a common sense of the word (Isaiah 5:14). The saying means: treat your appetite as if a blade were held to it. At a ruler's table greed could cost a young official his place, or show the host that he could be bought. The Greek translator did not render the knife at all (see the variant).
orig: בַּעַל נֶפֶשׁ (ba'al nefesh), 'owner of an appetite'

a: for that bread tells lies
p: The ruler's food is not what it seems: it comes with strings attached.
b: The Hebrew is "bread of lies" (lechem kezavim). The meal looks like generosity, but it may be a test of your self-control, a way to put you in the ruler's debt, or a chance to watch you when your guard is down. Joseph tested his brothers at a meal (Genesis 43:31–34), and Daniel refused the king's food so as not to be bound to it (Daniel 1:8). The same Hebrew line, "do not crave his fine foods", returns in 23:6, where the host is a stingy man instead of a ruler, and the Plain gives both the same words.

a: Let your understanding tell you to stop.
t: Stop using your understanding, or use it to stop?
p: The Hebrew says only "from your understanding, stop", and it can be read two ways.
b: The line is three Hebrew words: "from your understanding (binah) cease." The KJV took it as "cease from thine own wisdom": stop trusting your cleverness, which only schemes for more money. Most modern readers take the preposition as "by" or "out of": let your understanding make you stop. Both fit the context of 23:4–5. The Plain follows the second, keeping binah as "understanding" as elsewhere in Proverbs (3:5 warns against leaning on your own understanding, using the same word).

a: Will you let your eyes fly to it? Then it is gone.
p: A pun: your eyes fly to wealth, and the wealth flies away.
b: The verb "fly" ('uf) opens and closes the verse. The written text (Ketiv) reads "do your eyes fly to it?"; the reading tradition (Qere) reads "do you make your eyes fly to it?" Either way, a glance at riches is a flight, and the riches answer by sprouting wings of their own. The bird is a nesher, which can be an eagle or a vulture; both soar out of sight. The Hebrew "and it is not" is abrupt on purpose: look, and it is gone.
orig: הֲתָעִיף עֵינֶיךָ בּוֹ וְאֵינֶנּוּ (hata'if 'eineikha bo ve'enennu)

a: It is sure to make itself wings
t: Riches with the wings of geese
p: Amenemope's seventh chapter says stolen riches make wings like geese and fly into the sky.
b: Amenemope warns against riches got by robbery: they will not stay the night in your house; the ground may swallow them, or "they have made for themselves wings like the geese, [and] have spread their wings and flown up into the sky" (Budge's translation, lines 177–178). The image in 23:5 is the same, with an eagle for the geese. This is one of the clearest parallels between the two works, and it is the kind of detail that made Adolf Erman, in 1924, argue that Proverbs depends on Amenemope. Proverbs widens the point: Amenemope speaks of stolen goods, Proverbs of wealth itself, however it is pursued.

a: a man with a grudging eye
p: "Evil of eye" is a Hebrew idiom for a stingy, begrudging person, not a magic curse.
b: The Hebrew is "evil of eye" (ra' 'ayin). In Proverbs the eye shows whether a person is generous: "good of eye" is the generous man (22:9), "evil of eye" is the man who resents every bite his guest takes (28:22). It is not the folk belief in an "evil eye" that brings bad luck, which some readers have found here. Jesus uses the same idiom: in the parable of the workers the owner asks, literally, "Is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15), meaning "Are you jealous because I am generous?"

a: For he is the kind who keeps score inside.
t: "As he thinketh in his heart, so is he"
p: A famous line from the KJV, but the Hebrew is about a stingy host counting the cost, not the power of thought.
b: The KJV's "For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he" became a motto of self-help writing, most famously James Allen's As a Man Thinketh (1903), which took it to mean that your thoughts make you who you are. In context the line describes the grudging host of 23:6: he says "Eat and drink!" but inside he is reckoning what each mouthful costs him. The Hebrew runs "as he reckons in himself, so he is"; the Plain folds the last words, ken hu, "so he is", into "he is the kind who". The rare verb sha'ar means "reckon, calculate" (a related noun means "measure, price" in later Hebrew and Aramaic). The Hebrew is hard, and the Greek read the consonants differently (see the variant), but no reading supports the self-help sense.
orig: כְּמוֹ־שָׁעַר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ כֶּן־הוּא (kemo sha'ar benafsho ken hu)

a: The scrap you ate you will throw up
p: Amenemope's eleventh chapter uses the same images of craving, the throat and vomiting, for a different situation.
b: Amenemope's eleventh chapter, in Miriam Lichtheim's translation, opens: "Do not covet a poor man's goods, / Nor hunger for his bread; / A poor man's goods are a block in the throat, / It makes the gullet vomit." Later in the chapter comes "The big mouthful of bread—you swallow, you vomit it." Its subject is greed toward a dependent's property. Budge, the first editor (1924), read the opening differently, as craving the dainty food of a glutton, which is "as a storm in the gullet" (his lines 257–259). Proverbs 23:6–8 takes over the images, craving the food, the throat and vomiting it up, but puts them in a different situation: a guest at a stingy host's table, who throws up what he ate and wastes his pleasant words. The shared images are strong, and some scholars think the throat image helps with the hard Hebrew of 23:7 (see the note there).

a: Do not talk where a fool can hear
p: Some listeners cannot be taught; Proverbs and Jesus both warn against wasting wisdom on them.
b: The fool here is the kesil, the dull, self-satisfied fool who scorns good sense. Proverbs says elsewhere that correcting a mocker only earns you insults (9:7–8), and 26:4–5 weighs when to answer a fool at all. Jesus says much the same with a harsher image: "Do not toss your pearls down in front of pigs" (Matthew 7:6). Amenemope's twenty-first chapter has a related warning not to "empty thy belly" (pour out your thoughts) before everyone (Budge, lines 436–437).

a: Do not shift the old boundary line
p: Family land was marked by stones; moving one in the night stole land from those least able to fight back.
b: Fields in Israel were marked by boundary stones, and each family's land was meant to pass down within the family (Numbers 27:1–11; 1 Kings 21:3). Moving a stone was quiet theft. The law forbids it, "Do not move your neighbor's boundary marker" (Deuteronomy 19:14), and curses whoever does it (Deuteronomy 27:17). In Babylonia, boundary stones (kudurru) carried curses on anyone who moved them. Amenemope's sixth chapter warns against moving the boundary markers and cheating "the estate of the widow" (Budge, line 129). The first line of this verse is the same Hebrew as the first line of 22:28, and the Plain gives it the same words. Some scholars have proposed reading 'almanah, "widow", for 'olam, "old" (literally "of long ago"), to match Amenemope and the orphans of the next line; no Hebrew manuscript has that reading.

a: For their redeemer is strong.
p: A redeemer was the relative who stepped in to rescue family; for orphans with no such relative, God takes the role.
b: A go'el, a family redeemer, bought back a relative's land or freedom and defended the family's rights (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:1–8). Orphans had no one to do this, so the sage names a stronger redeemer: in the Hebrew Bible this is God, who is "a father to orphans" (Psalm 68:5) and whose "redeemer is strong" is said of him in nearly the same words in Jeremiah 50:34. The second line is a lawsuit image: he will "argue their case" (yariv rivam) against the thief, as at 22:23. Amenemope's parallel chapter puts the land-thief under the power of the moon god; Proverbs puts him in court against the LORD.

a: Bring your heart to discipline
t: A new start after the Egyptian parallels
p: Here the clear parallels to Amenemope end, and a fresh call to listen opens the next set of sayings.
b: The verse sounds like the opening of the whole collection: "Lean in and listen to the words of the wise" (22:17). Many scholars treat it as a new heading. After it, the parallels to Amenemope stop, and the next sayings (on the rod, 23:13–14) are closer to the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar. The key word is musar, "discipline": the training that includes teaching, correction and, in the next verses, punishment. On this site musar is always "discipline" (see the note at 1:2), so the reader can see the word link 23:12, 13 and 23 with 24:32.

a: Do not hold back discipline from a youth.
p: The Hebrew na'ar is a boy or young man, often a teenager, not a small child.
b: The word na'ar covers ages from a baby boy (Exodus 2:6) to a young man old enough for war or service (Genesis 37:2, Joseph at seventeen; 1 Samuel 17:33, David). In Proverbs the "youth" is the teenager or young man being trained for adult life (1:4; 7:7; 22:6). This matters for readers today: the verse is not chiefly about toddlers. It tells the father or teacher not to "hold back" (timna') discipline, the same verb used of holding back good from someone who deserves it (3:27). The point is that withholding discipline is a failure of love, as 13:24 says.
orig: אַל־תִּמְנַע מִנַּעַר מוּסָר ('al timna' minna'ar musar)

a: When you hit him with the rod
p: The Aramaic Story of Ahiqar has the same advice, with the same promise that the boy will not die.
b: The Story of Ahiqar, a court tale with sayings, circulated in Aramaic by the 400s BC (a copy was found at Elephantine in Egypt) and later in Syriac, Armenian and Arabic. Its oldest form, the Aramaic papyrus, has a saying almost identical to this one. In the translation printed in R. H. Charles's edition (1913), with gaps in the damaged papyrus marked: "Do not withhold thy son from beating, if thou . . . My son, if I beat thee, thou diest not. And if I leave on thy heart . . ." Later versions keep it. The Syriac: "My son, withhold not thy son from stripes; for the beating of a boy is like manure to the garden." The Armenian (Charles, from the Venice text): "For if thou strike him with a rod once or twice, he is rendered clever quietly, he does not die. But if thou leave him to his own will, he becomes a thief; and they take him to the gallows and to death." The match suggests a saying widely shared in the region rather than a direct copy.

a: he will not die
p: It may mean the beating will not kill him, or that discipline saves him from an early death.
b: The Hebrew ki can mean "for", "if" or "when", and lo yamut is "he will not die." Read one way, the line reassures a soft-hearted parent: a beating with the rod will not kill him, so do not be afraid to correct him. Read another way, it is a promise: if you discipline him he will not die, that is, he will not come to the early death that waits for the foolish and the wicked (5:23; 10:21; 19:16). The next verse, "you will rescue his life from Sheol", favors the second reading, and the Story of Ahiqar (see the previous note) puts "if I beat thee, thou diest not" beside the warning that the unbeaten son comes to the gallows.

a: It is you who hit him with the rod
t: How the rod sayings have been read
p: Teachers have read the rod sayings as a command, as a command with strict limits, or as a practice of their time.
b: Proverbs speaks of the rod in 10:13, 13:24, 22:15, 23:13–14, 26:3 and 29:15. Readers differ on how to apply it. As a direct command: many Christian teachers, such as James Dobson (Dare to Discipline, 1970), have taught measured physical punishment of children from these verses. With strict limits: the Talmud tells a teacher to strike a pupil only with a shoe strap (Bava Batra 21a) and condemns a father who strikes a grown son, since it provokes him to sin (Moed Katan 17a); Maimonides lets a teacher strike pupils to instill awe, but not cruelly, and only with a small strap, not a stick or a whip (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Torah Study 2:2). As a practice of its time: William Webb and others argue that the rod texts speak of beating youths, with no limit on strokes, in ways no modern advocate follows, and that the Bible's direction of travel points beyond them. The chapter page sets out these views. The Plain does not soften the text: the Hebrew says to hit him with the rod.

a: you will rescue his life from Sheol
p: Sheol is the world of the dead; here the rescue is from an early death, not a teaching about hell.
b: Sheol is the Hebrew name for the world of the dead, where all go at death (1:12; 5:5; 7:27). In Proverbs it stands for death that comes too soon, the end of the fool's road. The promise is that discipline now will keep the young man from that end. The KJV's "deliver his soul from hell" made the line sound like a promise of eternal salvation, and some preachers have used it that way; the Hebrew speaks of his life (nefesh) and of death. The Greek renders Sheol here as "death" (ek thanatou).

a: My insides will exult
p: The Hebrew says "my kidneys will exult": the kidneys stood for the deepest feelings.
b: Hebrew places feelings in the body. The kidneys (kilyot) are the hidden center of emotion and conscience, which God tests (Psalm 7:9; Jeremiah 17:10). A father's kidneys "exulting" means he is glad to the core. The Plain says "insides" so the image of the body stays without sounding strange in English. The verse pairs with 23:15: a wise heart in the son, a glad heart in the father; honest lips in the son, glad kidneys in the father.

a: be jealous instead for the fear of the LORD, all day long
p: The Hebrew leaves the verb out of the second line; the same word means both envy and zeal.
b: The verb qinne' means "be jealous, envy" and also "be zealous." The second line has no verb of its own: "but in the fear of the LORD all the day." Some supply "be" or "live" (live in the fear of the LORD). Others carry the first verb over: do not burn with envy of sinners, burn instead with zeal for the fear of the LORD. The Plain takes the second reading, which keeps the play on one word. The theme returns at 24:1 and 24:19 and in Psalm 37:1 and Psalm 73:3. On "the fear of the LORD", see the note at 1:7.
orig: אַל־יְקַנֵּא לִבְּךָ בַּחַטָּאִים ('al yeqanne' libbekha bachatta'im)

a: Then there will be a future for you
p: The word for "future" means what comes after, the outcome of a life.
b: 'Acharit is "the after": the end or outcome of something. Proverbs promises the one who fears the LORD a good outcome and denies one to the wicked: 23:18 and 24:14 say there is an 'acharit and that hope will not be cut off; 24:20 says the evil person has no 'acharit. Jeremiah 29:11 joins the same two words, "a future and a hope." Whether this future lies only in this life or beyond it is not said here; later Jewish and Christian readers heard both.

a: Do not keep company with wine-swillers
p: The pair of words recalls the rebellious son of Deuteronomy, and the insult thrown at Jesus.
b: The two words of 23:20–21, sove' (heavy drinker) and zolel (glutton), appear together in the law of the stubborn and rebellious son, whose parents tell the elders, "He is a glutton and a drunkard" (Deuteronomy 21:20). In the gospels Jesus' critics call him "a man who overeats and drinks too much, a friend of tax collectors and sinners" (Matthew 11:19; Luke 7:34). The Greek of Matthew uses oinopotēs, "wine-drinker", the word the Greek Proverbs uses in 23:20. The insult cast him as the rebellious son of the law; Jesus answers that wisdom is proved right by what she does.

a: Do not look down on your mother because she has grown old.
t: Honor that lasts into old age
p: The command to honor parents does not end when they grow old and weak.
b: The fifth commandment, honor your father and your mother (Exodus 20:12), is the background here. The sage adds the hard case: a mother whose age makes her easy to dismiss. The verb buz, "despise, look down on", is the same word used of the fool who despises wise words in 23:9. Sirach expands the thought: take care of your father in his old age, and do not grieve him even if his mind fails (Sirach 3:12–13). Paul and Jesus both press the command on adult children (Mark 7:10–13; 1 Timothy 5:4).

a: Buy truth, and do not sell it:
t: A verse the Greek does not have
p: This saying is missing from the Old Greek translation and may have been added to the Hebrew collection later.
b: The Old Greek (Rahlfs; Codex Vaticanus in Swete's edition) goes straight from 23:22 to 23:24. Some scholars think 23:23 was added to the Hebrew after the Greek translation was made, since it breaks the run of sayings on parents (23:22, 24–25). Others think the Greek translator dropped it. Its ideas are at home in Proverbs: "buy wisdom, buy understanding" (4:5, 7), and do not sell what is beyond price (8:10–11). The list "wisdom, discipline and understanding" uses three of the book's key words. The Plain follows the Hebrew, which has the verse in every manuscript.
orig: אֱמֶת קְנֵה וְאַל־תִּמְכֹּר ('emet qeneh ve'al timkor)

a: A righteous man's father will shout for joy
t: The son who makes his parents glad
p: A theme that frames the Solomon collection returns: a wise child is a parent's joy.
b: The first Solomon collection opens, "A wise son makes a father glad" (10:1), and the thought recurs (15:20; 17:21, 25; 27:11; 29:3). Here it is doubled for emphasis: the Hebrew gil yagil, "rejoicing he will rejoice", and the next verse adds the mother who bore him. In the reading tradition (Qere) the second line begins "and one who fathers"; the written text (Ketiv) differs only in spelling and a joining word. The appeal is warm: the son's wise life is a gift he gives back to his parents.

a: a foreign woman
p: The 'strange' or 'foreign' woman of Proverbs is a woman outside a man's marriage; see the note at 2:16.
b: The Hebrew nokhriyyah is the feminine of "foreigner", and this site keeps it as "foreign woman" throughout Proverbs (with zarah, "the strange woman"). Scholars differ on whether she is an actual foreigner, any woman married to another man, or a figure for Folly (9:13–18); see the note at 2:16. This verse pairs her with a prostitute (zonah). The warning is addressed to a young man and pictures women only as danger. Many modern readers, Jewish and Christian, point out that the book's other women, Wisdom, the mother who teaches (1:8; 31:1), and the woman of strength (31:10–31), complete the picture.

a: a deep pit
t: The pit and the narrow well
p: Both images are traps: a deep pit cannot be climbed out of, and a narrow well holds you fast.
b: A pit (shuchah) was dug to trap animals, and a well with a narrow mouth (be'er tsarah) is hard to escape once you fall in. The same words, shuchah 'amuqqah, "a deep pit", are used of "the mouth of strange women" in 22:14, and the Plain gives them the same English. Pit and well also suggest the grave and Sheol (1:12; Psalm 28:1). The image is the reverse of 5:15–18, where a man's own wife is his well and fountain. The Greek has a different line: "a strange house is a jar with holes". Where the Hebrew has zonah, "prostitute", the Greek has allotrios, "strange", which may mean the translator read zarah, "strange woman", the word of 2:16 and 22:14 (see the variant).

a: She too crouches in hiding like a robber
p: The rare word chetef probably means a robber; the KJV took it as the prey she waits for.
b: Chetef is found only here. It comes from a root "seize, snatch" (Job 9:12). Most modern readers take it as "robber", someone who snatches; the KJV took it as "a prey", what is snatched. The second line is also unclear: she "adds" or "multiplies" the bogedim, the treacherous or unfaithful, among men. That may mean she makes men unfaithful to their wives, or that she adds them to her list of victims. The Plain takes the first.

a: Who cries "Oh!"? Who cries "Alas!"?
p: The first two questions use cries of pain; the second is found nowhere else in the Bible.
b: The poem opens with six questions, a riddle whose answer comes in 23:30. The first two words are cries: 'oy, "woe!" or "oh no!" (the word behind the Yiddish "oy"), and 'avoy, found only here, probably a stronger form of the same cry. The Latin Vulgate read the letters differently: "whose father has woe?" Next come quarrels (the reading tradition's midyanim; the written text medonim, the same word spelled differently), grumbling, needless wounds and dark or bleary eyes. The questions are funny and sad at once: the drinker earns every symptom.

a: Who has bleary eyes?
p: The rare word may mean red, dull or darkened eyes; Genesis 49:12 uses its root for eyes dark with wine.
b: The noun chakhlilut appears only here. Its root is used in Jacob's blessing of Judah, whose eyes are dark (or sparkling) "from wine" (Genesis 49:12). Translators guess "redness" (KJV), "dullness" or "dark" (bruised) eyes. The Greek reads "livid" eyes, the color of a bruise. Whatever the exact shade, the reader is meant to see the morning-after face.

a: the mixed wine
p: Wine was often mixed with spices or with water; here the drinkers go looking for a strong blend.
b: The word mimsakh is a "mixture" of wine. Wine could be mixed with water to dilute it, as Greeks did, or with spices and herbs to make it stronger and more fragrant (Song of Songs 8:2). In 9:2 and 9:5 Wisdom herself "mixes her wine" for her guests, so mixing is not bad in itself. Here the drinkers "come to examine" it, like connoisseurs sampling the bowls, and they "sit late", staying until all hours. Isaiah mocks those who are heroes at mixing strong drink (Isaiah 5:11, 22).
r: 9:2; 9:5; Isaiah 5:11; Isaiah 5:22; Psalm 75:8; Song of Songs 8:2

a: as it shows its gleam in the cup
p: The Hebrew says the wine "gives its eye" in the cup: its sparkle catches yours.
b: The verb yit'addam means "shows itself red." Then the wine "gives its eye in the cup": the gleam on the surface, like an eye that catches yours. The written text (Ketiv) has kis, "purse", instead of kos, "cup"; the reading tradition reads "cup" (see the variant). The last line, that it "goes along smoothly", is used of good wine in Song of Songs 7:9. The verse admits what is attractive about wine before it warns of what follows.

a: like a viper, it strikes
p: No one is sure what the viper does: sting, spit poison or pierce.
b: The verb yafrish is rare. It may come from a root "spread out" (as poison spreads), or from one meaning "pierce, sting" (the KJV's "stingeth"). The snake is a tsif'oni, a kind of viper (Isaiah 11:8). The Plain uses "strikes", which fits a snake without claiming more than we know. The Greek says that "its poison is spread through him as by a horned snake."

a: Your eyes will see what is strange
p: The Hebrew "strange" is feminine plural; the KJV, the Greek and the Latin took it as strange women.
b: Zarot can mean "strange things" (the visions of the drunk) or "strange women", the plural of zarah, the "strange woman" of 2:16, 5:3 and 22:14. The Greek ("when your eyes see a strange woman"), the Vulgate and the KJV take it as women, linking drink and loose sex as 23:27–28 does just before. Most modern translations take it as hallucinations or confused perceptions, to match the twisted talk of the second line. Both senses may be meant. The Plain keeps "strange", the site's word for zar, so that the link can be seen.

a: on the top of a ship's mast
t: Asleep at the top of the mast
p: The rare word chibbel is probably a ship's mast or rigging: the drunk's bed sways like a ship.
b: Chibbel appears only here. It is related to chovel, "sailor" (Jonah 1:6), and so probably means the mast or the ropes of a ship. The picture is of a man who lies down and finds the room heaving like the open sea, or who is as careless of danger as a man asleep at the top of a mast. The Greek turns him into "a ship's pilot in a great storm."

a: I'll go hunting for it again.
p: The drinker cannot feel his injuries, and his first thought on waking is the next drink.
b: The poem ends in the drinker's own words. He was hit and beaten and felt nothing, and his first question on waking is not "What happened?" but when he can drink again. Modern readers often call this the Bible's clearest picture of addiction: pain without lesson, and craving that returns. The KJV adds "shalt thou say" in italics, as the Plain adds "You will say." In the 1800s the temperance movement used 23:29–35 widely, and 23:31 ("Do not stare at the wine") was read by many as a command to abstain. Others read it as a warning against the drinking that ends this way. The chapter page sets out how churches answer.

a: Do not be jealous of people who do evil
p: The third warning in a short space against envying evildoers; Psalm 37 and Psalm 73 wrestle with the same temptation.
b: The words of the wise return to this temptation three times: 23:17, 24:1 and 24:19. The young official sees that people who cut corners do well and wants to join them. The answer is the same each time: they have no future. Psalm 37 begins, "Do not burn up inside over people who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong" (Psalm 37:1), and Psalm 73 tells of a man who nearly slipped because he envied the proud. Proverbs 3:31 also says, do not envy a violent man.

a: A house is built with wisdom
p: The three words that build a house here are the same three by which God made the world (3:19–20).
b: 24:3–4 uses three key words in turn: wisdom (chokmah) builds the house, understanding (tevunah) makes it firm, knowledge (da'at) fills its rooms. In 3:19–20 God founded the earth "by wisdom", set the heavens "by understanding", and split the deeps "by his knowledge." The same triad fills Bezalel, who built the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3; Exodus 35:31). So a well-run household is a small copy of God's own work. The "house" may be a building, a household or a family line; Wisdom builds her house in 9:1 and a wise woman builds hers in 14:1.

a: where advisers are many, there is rescue
p: The second line repeats 11:14 word for word, and the first repeats 20:18.
b: The Hebrew of the second line is identical to the second line of 11:14, so the Plain gives it the same words. The first line is nearly the same Hebrew as the second line of 20:18, so the Plain matches it too: "with skilled steering" you make war. 15:22 makes the same point about plans in general. A saying could be reused in a new setting: here, after 24:5 on the strength of the wise, it means that brains win wars more than muscle. Ecclesiastes 9:13–18 tells of a poor wise man who saved a city. The word for "rescue" (teshu'ah) also means victory or salvation.

a: Wisdom is out of a stubborn fool's reach
p: The word for "too high" sounds like the word for coral: wisdom is both lofty and precious.
b: Ra'mot, "high things", is spelled like the word for coral, a costly import (Job 28:18; Ezekiel 27:16). The pun may be meant: wisdom is too high and too costly for this fool. He is the 'evil, the "stubborn fool" who will not be taught (on the word, see the note at 1:7). In the city gate, where elders judged cases and men of standing spoke (31:23), he has nothing to say. The Greek has a different verse: "Wisdom and good thought are in the gates of the wise."

a: master schemer
p: 24:8–9 plays on one root: a master of schemes, and the scheme of folly.
b: The Hebrew ba'al mezimmot is "a master (owner) of schemes." In 1:4 and 2:11 mezimmah is good "discretion"; here, in the plural and with ba'al, it is plotting. The next verse uses the same root: zimmat 'ivvelet, "the scheme of folly." A man becomes known by what he plans, and the name sticks. On this site mezimmah is "discretion" in its good sense and "schemes" in its bad sense.

a: your strength is too slim
p: The Hebrew plays on tsarah, 'trouble', and tsar, 'narrow': in a tight spot your strength is tight.
b: The day of trouble is yom tsarah, literally a day of narrowness, a tight place. Your strength is then tsar, narrow or small. English cannot keep the pun fully. The point is a challenge rather than a comfort: strength that fails under pressure was never much strength. The verse may also lead into 24:11–12, where a crisis tests whether you will act.

a: Rescue the people being hauled off to their deaths
p: The verse may mean innocent people led to execution, captives led away to slaughter, or anyone in mortal danger.
b: The people "taken to death" and "tottering toward the slaughter" are not named. Readers have taken them as: the unjustly condemned, led out to execution after a false trial, whom an official could save by speaking up (compare 31:8–9 and Susanna's rescue by Daniel in the Greek Daniel); war captives or the oppressed, carried off to be killed; or anyone in danger of death, as the Talmud's duty to rescue extends Leviticus 19:16, "do not stand by your neighbor's blood" (Sanhedrin 73a). It has also been cited for many modern causes; the anti-abortion "rescue" movement of the 1980s, Operation Rescue among them, took its name and language from verses like this one. The verse does not say who; it says you may not stand aside.

a: if only you would hold them back!
t: A wish, an oath or a condition?
p: The Hebrew 'im tachsokh can be read as 'if only you would hold them back' or as 'if you hold back' from rescuing them.
b: The particle 'im usually means "if." The KJV read the verse as the start of a long condition running on into 24:12: "If thou forbear to deliver them... if thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not." Many modern readers take 'im here as a wish ("if only you would...") or as a strong command ("surely hold them back"), since chasakh, "hold back", is used of restraining someone from harm. The Greek adds "do not spare" (yourself, or your effort). The Plain takes it as a wish, which keeps the urgency.

a: the one who weighs hearts
p: Egyptians pictured the dead man's heart weighed on scales; Proverbs gives the scales to the LORD, here and now.
b: In Egyptian belief the heart of a dead person was weighed against the feather of Maat (truth and order) before Osiris, as pictured in the Book of the Dead, chapter 125. Amenemope speaks of the ape of the god Thoth sitting by the scales, "[and] his heart [acts] as the tongue (or, pointer) thereof" (Budge, lines 336–337). Proverbs says three times that the LORD "weighs" hearts or spirits (16:2; 21:2; 24:12), using tokhen, "measure, weigh." The image is shared, but the theology differs: there is one judge, he weighs the living as well as the dead, and his judgment needs no magic spells.

a: he will give every human being what his deeds deserve
p: A line repeated through Scripture, from Psalm 62:12 to Romans 2:6 and Revelation 22:12.
b: The phrase "pay back a person according to his work" is a fixed formula. Psalm 62:12 says to God, "you pay each person back by what he does." Job 34:11, Jeremiah 17:10 and 32:19 use it, and in the New Testament it becomes the standard statement of final judgment: Paul says that God "will pay back each person according to his works" (Romans 2:6), and Jesus says the Son of Man will repay each by what he has done (Matthew 16:27; Revelation 22:12). In the Greek of Proverbs this verse reads almost word for word like Romans 2:6. Note how 24:29 uses the same formula: God repays by deeds; you may not.
r: Psalm 62:12; Job 34:11; Jeremiah 17:10; Jeremiah 32:19; Matthew 16:27; Romans 2:6; 2 Timothy 4:14; Revelation 22:12; 24:29

a: Look, we didn't know about this
t: "I do not know this man" (Claude's observation)
p: Claude's observation: the Greek excuse in this verse uses the words Peter later uses to deny Jesus.
b: In the Greek Proverbs the excuse for not rescuing the condemned is Ouk oida touton, "I do not know this one." When Jesus was being led to death, Peter said, Ouk oida ton anthrōpon, "I do not know the man" (Matthew 26:72; compare Mark 14:71). This is Claude's own observation, offered as a possibility; it is not a common reading in the commentaries, and the gospel writers do not cite Proverbs here. If it is more than chance, the scene of Peter's denial is the very failure that 24:11–12 warns against: someone being taken away to die, and a bystander saying he does not know him.

a: My son, eat honey, because it is good
p: Honey is a picture of wisdom: good for you and sweet to taste.
b: Honey was the sweetest food Israel knew, and the land was "flowing with milk and honey." The verse is set up as a comparison: eat honey, for it is sweet; know that wisdom is like that for your soul (24:14). Psalms say the same of God's words: sweeter than honey from the comb (Psalm 19:10; Psalm 119:103), and Ezekiel eats a scroll that tastes like honey (Ezekiel 3:3). Proverbs also warns that too much honey makes you sick (25:16, 27), a reminder that the image is about taste and not excess.

a: Wicked man
p: Proverbs rarely speaks to the wicked directly; some read "like a wicked man" instead.
b: The Hebrew has rasha', "wicked", with no preposition. Most take it as a direct address: "Do not lie in wait, you wicked man." That is unusual in a book that speaks to "my son." Others think "like" is understood: do not lie in wait like a wicked man. The verse ends with the reason in 24:16: you cannot keep a righteous person down. The Greek has a different saying: "Do not bring a wicked man into the pasture of the righteous, and do not be fooled by a full belly."

a: Seven times a righteous person falls, and up he gets
p: The "fall" is into trouble, not into sin; the familiar "seven times a day" is not in the text.
b: In context, falling is a disaster that the wicked plot (24:15), not a moral lapse. The point is resilience: the righteous person may be knocked down again and again ("seven" means many times), but rises; the wicked stumble once and stay down. Medieval preachers often quoted the Latin as "the righteous falls seven times a day" and applied it to small daily sins, and the phrase is still quoted that way; the words "a day" are not in the Hebrew or in the Vulgate ("septies enim cadet iustus et resurget"). Micah 7:8 and Psalm 37:24 have the same hope.
orig: שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק וָקָם (sheva' yippol tsaddiq vaqam)

a: do not be glad
t: "When your enemy falls": the Jewish reading
p: The Mishnah puts this verse in the mouth of Samuel the Small, and the rabbis built a teaching on it.
b: In the Mishnah, the sage Shmuel ha-Katan (Samuel the Small) gives 24:17–18 as his whole teaching (Avot 4:19). The rabbis applied the thought even to Israel's oppressors. The Talmud says that when the Egyptians drowned in the sea, the angels wanted to sing, and God said, "My handiwork is drowning in the sea, and you sing?" (Sanhedrin 39b; Megillah 10b). The custom of removing drops of wine from the cup at the Passover meal while naming the plagues is often explained the same way, as a lessening of joy at the suffering of others. Job 31:29 also counts joy at an enemy's ruin as a sin.

a: keep your heart from cheering
t: From gloating to loving the enemy
p: The Old Testament already forbids gloating over an enemy; Jesus goes further and commands love.
b: The law tells an Israelite to return an enemy's straying ox (Exodus 23:4) and to help unload a hater's donkey (Exodus 23:5). Job swears he was never glad when someone who hated him was ruined (Job 31:29). Proverbs 25:21–22, which Paul quotes in Romans 12:20, tells you to feed a hungry enemy. Jesus takes the last step: "keep loving your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44). The ethic grows across Scripture, but 24:17 is already a hard teaching: not just do no harm, but feel no glee.
r: Exodus 23:4–5; Job 31:29; 25:21–22; Romans 12:20; Matthew 5:43–48; Luke 6:27–36; 1 Corinthians 13:6

a: and turn his anger away from your enemy
p: Do not gloat, the verse says, or God may stop punishing your enemy. Readers have struggled with the motive.
b: Taken at face value, the reason sounds self-interested: do not gloat, or the LORD may let your enemy off. Readers have answered in several ways. God's anger turns to you: many Jewish and Christian commentators read the line as implying that God will turn his anger from your enemy onto you, since gloating is itself a sin. Judgment belongs to God: gloating claims a share in a judgment that is God's alone, and God refuses to let anyone enjoy it (Deuteronomy 32:35). A realistic first step: the sage meets the young man where he is; if you want justice done, do not spoil it with glee. The verse opens with pen, "or else", so the Plain says "or the LORD will see it": a warning, not a possibility. The Plain adds "your enemy" to make clear whom "him" means; the Hebrew says only "from him."

a: Do not burn up inside over people who do evil
p: The first line is word for word the opening of Psalm 37.
b: The Hebrew 'al titchar bamere'im is exactly the opening of Psalm 37, so the Plain uses the same words: "Do not burn up inside over people who do evil" (Psalm 37:1). The verb hitchar means to get hot, to fret or fume. The second line differs slightly: the psalm has "those who do wrong", Proverbs "the wicked." Both give the same reason, that the wicked have no future: they wither like grass (Psalm 37:2), their lamp goes out (24:20). Psalm 37 is itself a wisdom psalm, built like a string of proverbs. The verb of the second line, qinne', is the one the Plain renders "be jealous" in 23:17 and 24:1; here it is "envy" so that the verse matches the Plain of Psalm 37:1, whose Hebrew is the same.

a: the lamp of the wicked will go out
p: A burning lamp in the house meant life and family going on; its going out meant the end of a line.
b: An oil lamp burned through the night in an Israelite house, and to say someone's lamp was put out meant his life and his family line had ended (2 Samuel 21:17; 1 Kings 11:36). The line repeats the second line of 13:9 word for word in Hebrew, and the Plain gives both the same words, "the lamp of the wicked will go out", as at 20:20, where it is used of the son who curses his parents. Bildad says the same of the wicked in Job 18:5–6. Its opposite is the "future" ('acharit) that the wicked do not have (24:20a) and the righteous do (23:18; 24:14).

a: Fear the LORD, my son, and fear the king.
p: Fear of God and respect for the king belong together in the court wisdom of Proverbs; 1 Peter 2:17 echoes the pair.
b: The Hebrew has one verb for both: "fear the LORD, my son, and the king." The Plain repeats "fear" so that the line reads clearly in English. Proverbs gives the king great honor: he speaks with divine judgment (16:10), his anger is like a lion's roar (19:12; 20:2). The sage still names the LORD first. 1 Peter 2:17 makes the pair into two commands, "Fear God. Give honor to the king", keeping "fear" for God alone. Ecclesiastes 8:2–5 also counsels obedience to the king. The chapter page sets out how churches answer the question of obeying rulers.

a: the two of them
p: Most readers think "the two of them" means the LORD and the king; some think it means the rebels and the faithful.
b: "Their disaster" ('eidam) can mean the disaster that comes on the rebels or the disaster that the LORD and the king send. "The two of them" (sheneihem) most naturally points back to the LORD and the king of 24:21: who knows what ruin they can bring? Some take it as the two groups, those who fear God and the king and those who rebel. The Greek understood "either of them" in 24:21 (see the variant there) and "the punishments from both" here. In the Greek, five more couplets about the king's tongue follow (see the variant).

a: These too are by the wise
t: A short appendix, and where the Greek puts it
p: 24:23–34 is a small second collection of sayings of the wise, and the Greek places it after part of chapter 30.
b: The heading gam 'elleh lachakhamim, "these too belong to the wise", marks a short supplement to the "words of the wise" of 22:17–24:22. It has no link to Amenemope and no "my son" address. Its sayings are about courts (24:23–26, 28–29), work (24:27) and laziness (24:30–34). In the Old Greek the order of the book's last chapters is different: after 24:22 (and five added couplets) come the words of Agur, 30:1–14; then these sayings of the wise, 24:23–34; then 30:15–33; then the words of Lemuel, 31:1–9; then chapters 25–29; then the woman of strength, 31:10–31. The chapter page explains what this may mean for how the book was put together. The Greek also reads the heading differently (see the variant).

a: Favoring one face over another in judgment is not good.
p: The Hebrew idiom "recognize faces" means playing favorites in court.
b: Hakker panim is "to recognize faces": to let a person's standing, wealth or connections decide the case. The law commands judges, "do not recognize faces in judgment" (Deuteronomy 1:17; Deuteronomy 16:19), and Leviticus 19:15 forbids favoring either the poor or the great. "Not good" is an understatement that means "very bad." The same saying opens 28:21, which adds that some will sin for a piece of bread. In Swete's notes, Codex Sinaiticus leaves this line out of the Greek. James 2:1–9 applies the rule to the church.

a: "You are righteous,"
p: In a court case tsaddiq and rasha' mean "in the right" and "guilty"; the Plain keeps the book's usual words.
b: Across Proverbs this site renders tsaddiq "righteous" and rasha' "wicked." In a lawsuit the words also mean the party who is in the right and the party who is guilty. A judge who tells the guilty man "You are in the right" acquits him. The Plain keeps "wicked" and "righteous" so the book's key words stay visible, but the setting is a verdict. Compare 17:15: acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent are both detestable to the LORD; and Isaiah 5:23. That whole peoples and nations curse such a judge shows how public and serious the crime is.
orig: אֹמֵר לְרָשָׁע צַדִּיק אָתָּה ('omer lerasha' tsaddiq 'attah)

a: Lips get a kiss
p: An honest answer is as welcome as a kiss, a sign of friendship and loyalty.
b: A kiss was a greeting between relatives and friends (Genesis 29:11; Genesis 33:4) and a sign of loyalty to a king (1 Samuel 10:1; Psalm 2:12). A kiss on the lips is mentioned only here and is rare in the ancient sources; it suggests close friendship. The sense is that a straight, honest reply, especially in court or council (24:23–25), is a mark of true friendship. Compare "Wounds from someone who loves you are true, / but kisses from someone who hates you come thick and fast" (27:6).

a: Afterward you can build your house.
t: First the field, then the house
p: Plainly, get your living in order before you build; the rabbis also read "house" as marriage, and as a picture of study.
b: In plain terms the saying is about order: secure your income from the fields before you build a house, or before you start a household ("build a house" can mean found a family, Ruth 4:11; Deuteronomy 25:9). The Talmud draws on this verse and on Deuteronomy 20:5–7 (a house, a vineyard, a wife) to teach that a man should first build a house and plant a vineyard and only then marry, and it also reads the three steps as a course of study: first Scripture, then Mishnah, then Talmud (Sotah 44a). The Greek turns the last line into "follow after me, and you will rebuild your house."

a: Do not take the stand against your neighbor for nothing.
p: The ninth commandment applied: no testimony against a neighbor without real cause.
b: "For nothing" (chinnam) means without cause, when he has done nothing to deserve it. The commandment forbids false witness against a neighbor (Exodus 20:16), and the law punished a false witness with the penalty he wanted for the accused (Deuteronomy 19:16–21). Proverbs returns to the false witness often (6:19; 12:17; 14:5; 19:5, 9; 25:18). The next verse shows a likely motive: revenge.

a: Will your lips lead people astray?
p: The Hebrew can be read as a question ('would you deceive?') or as a second command ('do not deceive').
b: The verb vahapitita ("and you will deceive" or "and you will entice") follows a command without its own "do not." The KJV supplies "not" and reads it as a command. Many read it as an indignant question, as the Plain does. The verb pitah is used of the enticing sinners in 1:10 and of a man who seduces a girl (Exodus 22:16): a false witness leads the court astray.

a: As he did to me, so I will do to him.
p: The words of the law of retaliation are turned into a private grudge, and forbidden.
b: "As he did, so it shall be done to him" is the very wording of the law of retaliation in Leviticus 24:19, a rule for judges setting a fair penalty. In this verse a private person uses it to justify his own revenge, and the sage forbids it. The law already said, "Do not take vengeance, and do not keep a grudge against the children of your people" (Leviticus 19:18), and 20:22 says to wait for the LORD. The second line repeats 24:12 on purpose: "what his deeds deserve" is God's to give, not yours. Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:38–44 and Paul's in Romans 12:17–19 follow this line.

a: I went by a lazy person's field
t: A lesson from a walk past a ruined farm
p: The teacher tells what he saw: a story-saying, like the scene at the window in 7:6–23.
b: Here the sage speaks in the first person, as in 7:6–23 and in Psalm 37:25, 35–36: I passed by, I saw, I learned. The lazy one ('atsel) is a stock figure in Proverbs (6:6–11; 26:13–16), and he is paired with a person "lacking heart" (chasar lev), that is, without sense. The Hebrew here says "a lazy man" and "a man lacking heart"; the Plain uses "person", as it does for the lazy one throughout the book. The scene ends with a lesson drawn from it (24:32) and a saying the reader already knows from 6:10–11 (24:33–34). The ruined vineyard recalls Isaiah's song of the vineyard, whose wall is broken down and which grows thorns and thistles (Isaiah 5:5–6).

a: thistles had sprung up over all of it
p: The two plant words are uncertain; both mean the weeds that take over untended land.
b: Qimmeshonim (thistles or nettles) and charullim (weeds, perhaps chickpea-like vetch or nettles) are hard to identify exactly. Both grow wild on neglected ground. Thorns and thistles are the mark of the cursed ground in Genesis 3:18 and of the abandoned vineyard in Isaiah 5:6. The stone wall (gader) kept animals out of the vines; once it fell, the vineyard lay open (Psalm 80:12).

a: A little sleep, a little drowsing
p: 24:33–34 repeats 6:10–11 almost word for word, as the moral of the story.
b: The sage ends his story with a saying already found in 6:10–11, after the lesson of the ant. The two Hebrew texts differ in three small ways in 24:34: mithallekh, "one walking about", for 6:11's kimhallekh, "like one walking about"; a spelling difference in the word for poverty (rishekha for re'shekha); and a plural "your wants" for the singular "your want". Because 24:34 has no "like" before the walker, the Plain's "like a drifter" follows 6:11; the sense is the same, so the Plain gives both places the same words. The words may be the lazy one's own excuse ("just a little more sleep"), which the sage then answers with the outcome. The Greek makes it his confession: "I doze a little, I sleep a little." Folding the hands is the posture of rest (Ecclesiastes 4:5).

a: like a man with a shield
t: The drifter and the man with a shield
p: Poverty arrives like a drifter on the road and like an armed raider: slowly, then all at once.
b: Mithallekh is "one who walks about": a tramp, a vagrant, or a highway robber. 'Ish magen is "a man of shield", an armed man. The two images may describe poverty creeping up step by step and then striking with force. The Greek translator read the second differently: want comes "like a good runner." The Plain uses the same words here as at 6:11.
